extracted.intended_audience: general readers and public-health-interested audience (public, journalists, students, non-specialist clinicians)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic, sectioned overview of the 2009 H1N1 (swine flu) pandemic covering history, virology, clinical features, diagnostics, treatment, prevention, public-health response, and controversies. Intended as a comprehensive summary rather than prescriptive guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmed diagnosis requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmed diagnosis of pandemic H1N1 flu requires testing of a nasopharyngeal, nasal, or oropharyngeal tissue swab from the patient. Real-time RT-PCR is the recommended test as others are unable to differentiate between pandemic H1N1 and regular seasonal flu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most people with flu symptoms do not need a test for pandemic H1N1 because results usually do not affect treatment. The U.S. CDC recommends testing only for people who are hospitalized with suspected flu, pregnant women, and people with weakened immune systems. When a more definitive determination is required, testing with rRT-PCR or virus isolation should be performed. The CDC later released a new RT-PCR panel with results available in four hours and reported 96% accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rapid influenza diagnostic tests (RIDT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid influenza diagnostic tests (RIDT) yield quick results (about 30 minutes) but have a high rate of false negatives and cannot reliably distinguish pandemic H1N1 from seasonal flu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of RIDT false negatives, the CDC advises that patients with illness compatible with novel influenza A (H1N1) but negative RIDT results should be treated empirically based on clinical suspicion, underlying conditions, severity, and risk for complications, and confirmed with rRT-PCR or virus isolation if needed. Some researchers have questioned widespread reliance on RIDTs as a public-health risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical diagnosis and early treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors should not wait for laboratory confirmation but make diagnosis based on clinical and epidemiological background and start treatment early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nikki Shindo (WHO) expressed regret at treatment delays caused by waiting for test results; clinicians are advised to start antiviral treatment when clinically indicated rather than awaiting lab confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiviral treatment recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Antivirals (oseltamivir or zanamivir) were recommended for those with more severe symptoms or those in an at‑risk group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A November 2009 NEJM article recommended that flu patients whose chest X-ray indicates pneumonia receive both antivirals and antibiotics. Early antiviral therapy is emphasized for hospitalized patients and high-risk groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibiotic use for suspected bacterial pneumonia
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients whose chest X-ray indicates pneumonia should receive both antivirals and antibiotics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary bacterial pneumonia is a recognized complication; clinicians should treat radiologically confirmed pneumonia with appropriate antibiotics in addition to antiviral therapy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspirin contraindication in children
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspirin and other salicylate products should not be used by people under 16 with any flu-type symptoms because of the risk of developing Reye syndrome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use acetaminophen (paracetamol) or ibuprofen for symptom relief in children and teenagers; avoid salicylates in this age group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of severe cases and need for escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: In severe cases, patients generally begin to deteriorate around three to five days after symptom onset, with rapid progression to respiratory failure sometimes within 24 hours, requiring immediate ICU admission and mechanical ventilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severe illness can occur in previously healthy people; clinicians should monitor for rapid deterioration, arrange immediate respiratory support, and admit to ICU when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaccine priority allocation (initial scarcity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because H1N1 vaccine was initially in short supply, the CDC recommended initial doses go to priority groups: pregnant women, people who live with or care for babies under six months old, children six months to four years old, and health-care workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different countries had somewhat differing priority lists (e.g., UK NHS prioritized people over six months who were clinically at risk, pregnant women, and households of immunocompromised people). Prioritization aimed to protect vulnerable groups and maintain healthcare capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaccine dosing and later universal recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical trials showed that adults were protected with only one dose instead of two; in February 2010 the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices voted for 'universal' flu vaccination in the United States to include all people over six months of age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vaccine effectiveness estimates varied by subgroup and region; distribution delays highlighted production and international distribution shortcomings. Studies later estimated vaccine impact in prevented illnesses and deaths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay-home and isolation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The CDC recommended that students, school workers, and persons with flu symptoms should stay home for seven days total, or until 24 hours after symptoms subsided, whichever is longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools were urged to suspend normal penalties (late‑paper penalties, doctor's-note requirements) to encourage self-isolation, designate rooms for symptomatic people waiting to go home, and plan for continuity (meals, lessons) if closures occurred. The same stay‑home guidance was applied to workplaces with advice to plan for remote work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace pandemic planning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers should consider and communicate objectives such as reducing transmission among staff, protecting people at increased risk of complications, maintaining business operations, and minimizing adverse effects on supply chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CDC estimated up to 40% of the workforce might be unable to work at the pandemic peak; employers were advised to plan for remote work, succession, and continuity measures and to communicate these plans to staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face mask use guidance (non-healthcare settings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. CDC did not recommend face masks or respirators in non-healthcare settings with exceptions: people who were ill around others, and people at risk for severe illness while caring for someone with the flu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There was disagreement among experts; some feared masks give a false sense of security. Mask use was common in parts of Asia for cultural/hygiene reasons. In healthcare settings different guidance applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and border control guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: On 7 May 2009 the WHO stated containment was not feasible and countries should focus on mitigating the effect of the virus; they did not recommend closing borders or restricting travel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some countries nonetheless adopted travel screening, quarantines, or import bans. Studies later showed airport screening for influenza symptoms was not an effective infection-control method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Airport screening and thermal imaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermal imaging cameras can detect elevated body temperature, one sign of swine flu, but studies found screening individuals at airports during the 2009 H1N1 outbreak was not an effective method of infection control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thermal screening may identify febrile passengers but misses asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic cases; authorities varied in applying such measures despite limited effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarantine use for incoming travellers (examples and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries quarantined or confined visitors suspected of having or being in contact with infected individuals (examples: China, Hong Kong, Japan, Australia), while others issued travel alerts or warnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quarantines were sometimes controversial and had diplomatic/social consequences; their use varied widely and often targeted perceived high-risk groups or vessels (cruise ships, hotels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and stigma-avoidance in terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: The WHO uses '(H1N1) 2009 pandemic' and officially adopted 'A(H1N1)pdm09' for the virus; criticism arose about informal names like 'swine flu' or 'Mexican flu' that could confuse the public or stigmatize communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Health authorities and international organisations recommended neutral, non‑stigmatizing nomenclature to avoid implying geographic or animal origins and to reduce public confusion and discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHO pandemic-declaration basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions to raise the level of pandemic alert and to declare a pandemic were based on virological and epidemiological criteria (spread beyond borders and a virus to which people have no immunity) rather than arbitrary or commercial considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics alleged WHO exaggerated the danger or was influenced by industry; WHO and its Director‑General defended that clearly defined criteria were used and later commissioned independent reviews of its handling of the pandemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food safety regarding pork and pigs
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading health agencies and the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture stressed that eating properly cooked pork or other food products derived from pigs will not cause flu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite reassurances, some governments implemented import bans or culling decisions; public messaging emphasized proper cooking and that pork consumption is not a transmission route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaccine-impact and effectiveness reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-pandemic studies estimated vaccine effectiveness and impact (e.g., overall effectiveness around 56–62% in some analyses and estimated lives saved), and retrospective assessments considered timing of vaccination campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses noted that earlier vaccine rollout could have prevented more cases; reporting of effectiveness varied by population subgroup and study methodology.
